# Ezekiel 21 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview

Ellicott notes this chapter contains three closely-connected prophecies, together called "the prophecy of the sword." The first (vv.2–7) restates in plain language the figurative denunciation of Ezekiel 20:45–49; the second (vv.8–17) repeats and intensifies it; the third (vv.18–27) adds circumstantial detail, closing (vv.28–32) with a prophecy against the Ammonites.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/21.htm

Enduring Word calls it "the sword song" and quotes Charles Feinberg: "No chapter in the Bible speaks more prominently and fully of the sword of the Lord than does this chapter."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-21/

---

## vv. 1–2: Setting the Prophet's Face

**v. 2 — "Set your face toward Jerusalem … preach against the sanctuaries"**

- **Gill (Baptist, 18th c.):** This identifies "the south" of Ezekiel 20:46 as Jerusalem. The "holy places" means the temple and its courts — the porch, the holy place, and the holy of holies. Synagogues in city and country are also included. Some rabbis thought both the first and second temple destructions were intended.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/21.htm

- **Ellicott (Anglican):** The expressions "set thy face," "drop thy word," "prophesy" and "say to the land" connect this plainly with Ezekiel 20:46–47, but now in literal terms — "Jerusalem," "the holy places," and "the land of Israel" replace the earlier figurative language.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/21.htm

- **Enduring Word (Pentecostal/charismatic):** It's a terrible thing to have God speak against a land so favoured as Israel. More pointedly, God declares "I am against you" — not just against the land, but against the people.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-21/

---

## vv. 3–5: The Sword Drawn — Righteous and Wicked Alike

**v. 3 — "I will draw My sword … cut off both the righteous and the wicked"**

- **Gill:** The sword is the Chaldean army coming out of Babylon — this interprets the "fire" of Ezekiel 20:47. The righteous and the wicked are the "green and dry tree" of the earlier parable. They may fall together in temporal calamities; the righteous are chastised or carried captive for their good (like Ezekiel and Daniel), the wicked are cut off by sword and famine. Gill also cites R. Saadiah Gaon who interpreted "righteous" as those who served Baal continually vs. those who served him only occasionally — both were wicked before the Lord.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/21.htm

- **Enduring Word (Pentecostal/charismatic):** Temporal judgment is indiscriminate — war recognises only victors and victims, with "no concern to subdivide the latter according to that nation's definitions of righteous and wicked" (quoting Block). This does not contradict Ezekiel 18:20 ("the soul who sins shall die"), which speaks of final judgment. In temporal judgments, both often suffer equally (Smith).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-21/

- **Pulpit Homiletics (broad Protestant):** The whole nation was corrupt and ripe for slaughter. The so-called "righteous" were only less tainted with sin in comparison with the blackest characters. In the nature of things, God does not treat the righteous and wicked alike, but so few were truly righteous that they are left out of this graphic description. The same outward calamity that sends a leaky ship to the bottom drives the tight ship home faster.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/ezekiel/21.htm

- **Ellicott:** These expressions show the universality of the desolation. God's actual separation of the righteous from the wicked was already set forth in Ezekiel 9:4–6, but in national judgments the innocent are necessarily involved in the same temporal sufferings. The general terms are to be limited by what is elsewhere said of the mercy shown to a remnant.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/21.htm

- **Peake's Commentary (modern scholarship):** Ezekiel sees that the fall of Jerusalem will involve this indiscriminate destruction, though this "rather conflicts with his theory of strict individual retribution which he had so fully expounded in ch. 18."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/ezekiel-21.html

**v. 5 — "It shall not return any more"**

- **Ellicott:** Other judgments upon Israel had been arrested in mercy — the sword returned to the scabbard while the work was incomplete. This one will go on to the end.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/21.htm

- **Benson (Methodist):** The sword will not return to its sheath until it has executed all God's purposes.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/ezekiel-21.html

---

## vv. 6–7: The Prophet's Groaning

**v. 6 — "Groan! … with a broken heart and bitter grief"**

- **Enduring Word:** The phrase "breaking of thy loins" (KJV) literally means "breaking loins." "Loins" in the OT are the seat of strength and emotions; when broken, strength is gone and one is helpless. God did not want an unemotional messenger — the prophet's heart must display God's own breaking heart.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-21/

- **Gill:** The prophet was to go as if his loins were broken, like a woman in travail, with hands on loins in utmost distress — sighing "before their eyes" so the captives in Babylon would notice and send word to Jerusalem.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/21.htm

- **Ellicott:** The loins were regarded as the seat of strength (Job 40:16); breaking them expresses entire prostration.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/21.htm

**v. 7 — "Every heart will melt … every knee will turn to water"**

- **Enduring Word:** The phrase "all knees will be weak as water" is a euphemism for loss of bladder control in moments of terror (Vawter and Hoppe). Trapp says "they shall bepiss themselves for fear, saith Jerome." It describes complete loss of control and dignity.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-21/

- **Gill:** The knees "shall flow with water" — either with sweat, or with urine, through fear.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/21.htm

---

## vv. 8–17: The Song of the Sword

**v. 10 — "It despises the scepter of My son"**

- **Enduring Word:** "My son" is probably Zedekiah, the ruler of Judah, or the nation itself. The sword of judgment had no regard for his right to reign — it would destroy his scepter as a metal sword destroys wood. Wiersbe: "Despising the king of Judah, the sword of Babylon would turn Judah's scepter into nothing but a stick!"
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-21/

- **Ellicott:** This refers to Genesis 49:9–10, where Jacob addresses Judah as "my son" and foretells the sceptre shall not depart until Shiloh comes. The true sense may be that the clause represents an objection from the Jew: "But 'the rod of my son' despiseth every tree" — i.e., the divine promise to Judah is sure, and his sceptre must remain. The objectors vainly imagined this gave temporal security whatever the nation's sins. The prophet doesn't answer the objection but simply continues his prediction of desolation.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/21.htm

- **Gill (alternative reading):** The words may be rendered "it is the rod of my son, it despiseth every tree" — this sword is the rod of iron with which the Son of God rules His enemies; no tree, high or low, can stand before it (cf. Psalm 2:7).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/21.htm

**v. 13 — "Surely testing will come!"**

- **Ellicott:** The Hebrew is obscure and abrupt. The most satisfactory translation: "For it (the sword) has been proved (on others), and what if this contemning rod shall be no more?" — i.e., Babylon's sword has already proven its power; the sceptre of Judah that despises it shall be swept away.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/21.htm

**v. 14 — "Let the sword strike two times, even three"**

- **Enduring Word (citing Clarke):** Nebuchadnezzar came against Judea three times: (1) against Jehoiakim, (2) against Jeconiah, (3) against Zedekiah. The sword had already been doubled; now it comes the third time.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-21/

- **Gill:** Some refer this to the three captivities (Jehoiakim, Jeconiah, Zedekiah); others to the three Chaldean incursions in Zedekiah's time.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/21.htm

- **Ellicott:** The exact translation is obscure, but the meaning is plain: the activity of the sword is to be intensified to the utmost. "The sword of the great men that are slain" — literally "the sword of the overthrown (plural), the sword of the overthrown (singular), of the great one" with special reference to the king.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/21.htm

**v. 16 — "Slash to the right; set your blade to the left"**

- **Ellicott:** The sword is addressed as a host: "Gather thyself up (close up ranks) right; set thyself, left" — an animation lost in the English version. God presents Himself as a general directing the thrust of the blade.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/21.htm

**v. 17 — "I too will strike My hands together, and I will satisfy My wrath"**

- **Ellicott:** God's fury "rests" because it has accomplished its purpose and has nothing more to do (cf. Ezekiel 5:13; 16:42).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/21.htm

- **Gill:** Some take it as God expressing indignation at sin; others as encouraging the enemy, even rejoicing at destruction for the honour of His justice. The Targum: "and even I will bring vengeance upon vengeance."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/21.htm

## vv. 18–23: Nebuchadnezzar at the Crossroads

**vv. 18–20 — "Mark out two roads for the sword of the king of Babylon"**

- **Ellicott:** The prophet is directed in vision to represent Nebuchadnezzar at the fork of the roads, hesitating between Jerusalem and Rabbah of the Ammonites. The whole is vivid, concrete imagery — it was a vision, not an actual event. The roads from Babylon to Rabbah and Jerusalem were the same for many hundreds of miles; the prophet could not have physically stood at their parting. "Choose thou a place" is literally "make a hand" — i.e., a finger-post or signpost.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/21.htm

- **Enduring Word:** "Make a sign" — the use of "yad" (lit. "hand") for signpost suggests a road sign with a carved hand pointing in the specified direction (Block). Rabbah is the modern Amman in Transjordan.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-21/

**v. 21 — "He shakes the arrows, he consults the idols, he examines the liver"**

- **Enduring Word:** Three real Babylonian divination practices: (1) Belomancy/rhabdomancy — shaking inscribed arrows and drawing one; (2) Consulting teraphim (household idols); (3) Hepatoscopy — examining the liver of sacrificed animals. Over all this, God was sovereignly determining Nebuchadnezzar's course.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-21/

- **Ellicott:** Arrow-shaking was practised among ancient Arabs and Mesopotamians, forbidden later by Mohammed in the Koran. The "images" were teraphim, small idols used in divination even by Israelites. Liver inspection (hepatoscopy) is familiar from classical literature and was practised in Babylonia. The king employs all these methods to "make sure" of the proper path — but God had already fixed it.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/21.htm

- **Gaebelein (Dispensational):** The Babylonians used different kinds of enchantments. The king put one arrow marked "Rabbath" and another "Jerusalem," shook them, and drew the Jerusalem arrow. God overruled it all.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/ezekiel-21.html

**v. 22 — "In his right hand appears the portent for Jerusalem"**

- **Ellicott:** The sense is "into his right hand came the divination which determined his course towards Jerusalem." The clauses portray siege operations: battering rams, opening the mouth in slaughter, shouting, siege mounds, and forts.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/21.htm

**v. 23 — "It will seem like a false omen … to those who have sworn allegiance"**

- **Ellicott:** The divination seemed false to the Jews because they were determined not to believe it, and because they were vassals of Babylon under solemn oaths of fidelity (Zedekiah was placed on the throne by Nebuchadnezzar under oath — 2 Chronicles 36:10–13). They persuaded themselves their intrigues with Egypt were unknown. But Nebuchadnezzar "will call to remembrance" their violation of oaths.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/21.htm

- **Pulpit Homiletics:** Though a heathen king who consulted augury, Nebuchadnezzar was truly God's instrument. God can guide even men's appeals to chance and overrule them for His own purpose (Proverbs 16:33).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/ezekiel/21.htm

## vv. 24–27: The Profane Prince and the Coming One

**v. 24 — "You shall be taken in hand"**

- **Ellicott:** The rebellion and perjury were only the last act of a long course of sin — when this last sin is exposed, sin is shown in all their doings.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/21.htm

**v. 25 — "O profane and wicked prince of Israel"**

- **Ellicott:** The word "profane" is the same as "slain" in v.14 — better rendered "overthrown." "The day has come for your final punishment" — literally "at the time of the iniquity of the end" — the final transgression that brings immediate divine judgment.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/21.htm

- **Gaebelein (Dispensational):** While Zedekiah is first in view, the prophecy looks far beyond him to the coming wicked prince — the final Antichrist, the false messiah of the time of the end. The phrase "in the time of the iniquity of the end" (correct translation) appears also in Daniel 11:35–39 referring to the Antichrist. This false Christ will claim both priestly and kingly honours.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/ezekiel-21.html

**v. 26 — "Remove the turban, and take off the crown"**

- **Enduring Word:** The turban (mitre) was the high priest's headdress (Exodus 28:37); the crown belonged to the king. Priesthood and royalty were both to be interrupted, set aside for a time (Feinberg). This signals the temporary removal of both offices from Israel.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-21/

- **Ellicott:** The word translated "diadem" in the KJV is everywhere else rendered "mitre" of the high priest. Not only the royal but also the high-priestly office was to be overthrown. Neither was ever recovered in full power after the exile.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/21.htm

- **Gaebelein (Dispensational):** The Antichrist will wear the mitre of the priest and the crown of the king — Satan's final counterfeit (like the pope) of the Priest-King. The two horns of the beast in Revelation 13 represent priesthood and kingship.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/ezekiel-21.html

- **Pulpit Homiletics:** "Exalt the lowly and bring low the exalted" — Jeconiah (the captive king) is probably meant; he was later exalted above all the captive kings in Babylon (2 Kings 25:27–29; Jeremiah 52:31).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/ezekiel/21.htm

**v. 27 — "A ruin, a ruin, I will make it a ruin! … until the arrival of Him to whom it belongs"**

This is the most commented-upon verse in the chapter.

- **Enduring Word (Pentecostal/charismatic):** One of the great Messianic promises of the OT, though often overlooked. After Zedekiah, no descendant of David would reign until Jesus the true Son of David comes. "From Zedekiah down to the Lord Jesus there has been no one in the line of David who ever sat on that throne" (McGee). The threefold "overthrown" reflects the three Babylonian subjugations of Jerusalem. The coming of the Lord for His church in the rapture is recalled in the Lord's Supper: "till He come." Israel also has an "until He come" — the Messiah will restore both priestly access and righteous royal rule (Feinberg).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-21/

- **Ellicott (Anglican):** This is generally acknowledged as a reference to Genesis 49:10 ("until Shiloh come"), even by those who reject "Shiloh" as meaning "he to whom it belongs." The condition following the overthrow will not be permanent — everything thrown into flux and change without permanent settlement "until he come whose right it is." The promise refers to both priestly and royal prerogatives; a more distinct foretelling of their union in the Messiah is in Zechariah 6:12–13. Daniel 7:14 confirms: "His dominion is an everlasting dominion."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/21.htm

- **F.B. Meyer (Holiness/Baptist devotional, via Precept Austin):** "Whatever the king of Judah thought to establish by his wit and power, God would overthrow. Nothing should stand, however carefully constructed, till the Messiah came to take up the kingdom and rule with meekness and righteousness." Meyer also applies the threefold overturning devotionally: "Our King is always engaged in destruction, that He may the better occupy Himself with construction. He overthrows our cities of brick, that He may build them of marble."
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel-f_b_meyer

- **Gill (Baptist):** The rod or sceptre shall be no more in one of David's line, of the tribe of Judah, until the Messiah comes.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/21.htm

- **Gaebelein (Dispensational):** Thrice stated: "I will overturn." This will be so at the time of the end, until He comes whose right it is. The Antichrist will be overturned.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/ezekiel-21.html

## vv. 28–32: Judgment on the Ammonites

**v. 28 — "Concerning the Ammonites and their contempt"**

- **Ellicott:** At vv.19–20, Nebuchadnezzar was shown hesitating between Jerusalem and Rabbah, and led to attack Jerusalem first. This could leave the inference that Ammon might escape. Hence this prophecy shows God's judgments will fall on them too — and their ruin is final and hopeless, without the promise given to Israel in v.27. Historically, the Ammonites were conquered by Nebuchadnezzar a few years after Jerusalem's fall and gradually vanished from history. "Their reproach" means their exultation in Israel's desolation (cf. Ezekiel 25:3; Zephaniah 2:8).
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/21.htm

- **Enduring Word:** The land of Ammon was east of the Jordan, in modern-day Jordan. The same "sword song" is sung against Ammon because they mocked and mistreated Judah in her collapse. Clarke notes the prophecy was fulfilled about five years after Jerusalem's fall (Josephus, *Ant.* x.11).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-21/

**v. 30 — "Return the sword to its sheath! … I will judge you"**

- **Ellicott:** The original has no question; it addresses the Ammonites: "Return it (the sword) into its sheath" — meaning all resistance is vain; the coming destruction cannot be averted. Judgment will be in their own land.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/21.htm

**v. 31 — "I will breathe the fire of My fury … brutal men, skilled in destruction"**

- **Ellicott:** The sword imagery is dropped for fire imagery (cf. Ezekiel 20:47; 22:21). God's wrath is blown by His power against Ammon like wind driving fire through a forest (cf. Isaiah 54:16). "Brutish" is better than the marginal "burning."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/21.htm

**v. 32 — "You will not be remembered"**

- **Enduring Word:** Unlike Israel, Ammon would eventually disappear as a people. Taylor: "Their ultimate fate will be worse than Israel's and worse even than Egypt's, for they will be no more remembered. To the Semitic mind nothing could be more terrible: no prospect of restoration, no continuance in succeeding generations, no memorial, not even a memory. Oblivion."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-21/

- **Ellicott:** For Ammon there should be no future, like that promised to Israel in v.27.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/21.htm

## Points of Denominational Difference

### The "righteous and wicked" problem (vv. 3–4)
- **Reformed/Ellicott/Anglican:** The innocent are necessarily involved in national temporal judgments; God's discriminating separation (Ezek 9:4–6) refers to final judgment. The remnant is still shown mercy.
- **Pulpit Homiletics (broad Protestant):** The whole nation was so corrupt that truly righteous people were statistically negligible — God does not ultimately treat righteous and wicked alike.
- **Peake (modern scholarship):** Notes a real tension with Ezekiel's theology of individual retribution in ch. 18.
- **Enduring Word (Pentecostal/charismatic):** Distinguishes temporal from final judgment. War is indiscriminate by nature.

### "The scepter of My son" (v. 10) and Messianic interpretation
- **Ellicott (Anglican):** Sees the phrase as an objection from the Jews based on Genesis 49:9–10 — they wrongly assumed the Davidic promise guaranteed present security regardless of sin.
- **Enduring Word/Gill (evangelical/Baptist):** Generally identify "My son" as Zedekiah or the nation, with the sword despising his royal authority.
- **Gaebelein (Dispensational):** Sees Antichrist typology in the "wicked prince" and the false priest-king.

### The "profane wicked prince" (vv. 25–27) — Zedekiah or Antichrist?
- **Traditional majority (Gill, Ellicott, Enduring Word, Pulpit):** Zedekiah is the primary referent. The "overturning" describes the historical fall of the Davidic monarchy until Christ.
- **Gaebelein (Dispensational):** While Zedekiah is first in view, the ultimate referent is the Antichrist — "the time of the iniquity of the end" points to the great tribulation. The false messiah will claim both priestly and kingly honours (like the beast of Revelation 13).
- **F.B. Meyer (Holiness/Baptist):** Applies the "overturning" devotionally to God's sanctifying work in the believer's life.

### v. 27 — The Messianic Promise
All Protestant traditions consulted agree this verse is a major Messianic prophecy fulfilled in Jesus Christ. The differences are in eschatological framework:
- **Dispensational (Gaebelein, McGee via Enduring Word):** Emphasises the literal future reign of Christ on David's throne, with the present church age as an "interruption" of the Davidic kingship.
- **Reformed/Amillennial (not found in specific chapter detail, but noted from Monergism on Ezekiel 40–48):** Would see Christ's present reign at the right hand of God as the fulfillment, with the consummation at the new creation. The Ligonier/Sproul overview emphasises God humbling His wayward people to renew their devotion.
— https://www.monergism.com/amillennial-interpretation-ezekiel-40-48 (on Ezekiel 40–48, but relevant to hermeneutical approach)
— https://learn.ligonier.org/series/dust-glory-old-testament/ezekiel-ot
